text: I used to manage OS level trust root management for all internal machines at a hyperscaler. Hundreds of thousands of machines. Even when you have an edict from a common VP or CEO, and most people are even using the same linux distributions, it's hard to get people to adhere to or even understand that there is a standard. Throw containers, embedded devices, windows and mac in and it's just a total nightmare unless you exert strict control on how every single machine is set up. Which, of course, is impossible because cowboys gonna cowboy. Fundamentally, people don't want to think about the intricacies of how we decide whether or not to trust a particular cert. They want it to just work without thinking about it. This includes that if they have a custom private root they need to trust, they just drop it various places until it starts working and call it done. And sometimes they do weird things like adding intermediates to their trust store because they were trying to call a service that has their cert chain configured incorrectly, and that "fixes it". Again, it's a nightmare. The fact that linux, a system notoriously cobbled together by 873 different factions on the internet, is even more of a mess is not surprising in the least.

It does just the same sort of thing a machine learning researcher would do to solve the problem. So there are basically two unrelated types of experiments in the paper. In one type of experiment, the model reads the weights like it reads an image. In fact if you visualise the weights it's fairly clear why this works. In the other type of experiment, the model is tasked with writing Python code to do ML engineering. This requires writing Python programs to analyse and manipulate weight data. text: Yes. Every 1970s videogame has some sort of scheduler that moves actors, draws the screen, and play sound. Depending on the computer, it might be very easy (some could interrupt when the VDP got to a specific spot) or require you to count cycles. If, for instance, your game is for an Apple II and you have background music, you need to hit the speaker at the frequency of the currently playing note WHILE you move things, do physics, and redraw the screen. And you need to count cycles, because there is no reliable counter you could use (I remember how awesome it'd be if I could write 0 to a memory location and read it later to know how many clock cycled passed, or one I could read to get which scan line of the image the video hardware was outputting).
